questions.prompt: A patient's chart lists 'Treponema pallidum' under 'cause' and 'chancre, rash, transmission by sexual contact' under 'course.' Which two branches of pathology are these?

options.text: Epidemiology and etiology
Etiology and immunology
Etiology and pathogenesis
Pathogenesis and epidemiology

questions.explanation: Etiology = cause; pathogenesis = how the disease develops.

questions.prompt: Which microbe–relationship–benefit set is correct?

options.text: E. coli — mutualism — makes vitamin K and bacteriocins
Vibrio cholerae — commensalism — neither helps nor harms
Candida — mutualism — makes vitamin K on the skin
S. epidermidis — parasitism — causes most staph infections

questions.explanation: E. coli in the colon is the course's mutualism example.

questions.prompt: Which statement about acquiring normal flora is FALSE?

options.text: S. epidermidis comes from nursing and handling.
The fetus picks up E. coli from the amniotic fluid.
E. coli comes from contaminated food and objects.
L. acidophilus comes from passing through the birth canal.
The microbiome approaches stability around age two.

questions.explanation: The amniotic sac is sterile; E. coli comes later from food and objects.

questions.prompt: Measles cases jump from 0 to 40 in one county within two weeks. Which pair of terms fits best?

options.text: Sporadic and subclinical
Epidemic and contagious
Pandemic and latent
Endemic and non-communicable

questions.explanation: Many cases in an area in a short time; measles spreads easily.

questions.prompt: Define incidence and prevalence, and explain what happens to prevalence if a new drug keeps patients alive longer without curing them.
questions.explanation: Incidence = new cases in a time period; prevalence = all (new + existing) cases at a given time. If patients live longer without a cure, fewer cases leave the 'jar,' so prevalence rises even if incidence is unchanged.

questions.prompt: Give three limitations of Koch's postulates with an example of each.
questions.explanation: Multiple causes (sinusitis, UTIs); microbes that can't be pure-cultured; ethical concerns with human-only pathogens (Koch's postulates have never been completed for HIV/AIDS). Barry Marshall avoided the ethics problem by infecting himself with H. pylori.

questions.prompt: A patient feels completely normal on day 6 of a 10-day antibiotic course. Which disease stage is he likely in, and what's the risk of stopping?

options.text: Incubation; the drug hasn't started working on the microbes yet
Convalescence; resistant survivors could restart the infection
Period of illness; stopping now won't change the outcome
Prodromal; his symptoms are about to peak in a day or two

questions.explanation: Signs and symptoms are gone before the microbe count reaches zero.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of infection term and example is correct?

options.text: Latent — food poisoning
Secondary — pneumonia after sinusitis
Subclinical — tuberculosis scarring the lungs
Local — measles

questions.explanation: Latent = herpes; local = abscess; subclinical = hepatitis A.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts direct and indirect contact transmission?

options.text: Direct goes through a fomite; indirect needs physical contact
Direct needs physical contact; indirect goes through a fomite
Direct is always airborne; indirect is always through water
Direct requires an arthropod vector; indirect requires a vehicle

questions.explanation: Fomites (doorknobs, toys, equipment) are the middlemen.

questions.prompt: Which portal of entry fits each case: a mosquito bite, a sneeze inhaled, a burn?

options.text: Broken skin; parenteral; mucous membrane
Mucous membrane; parenteral; broken skin
Parenteral; mucous membrane; broken skin
Parenteral; broken skin; mucous membrane

questions.explanation: Bites plunge through intact skin; inhaled droplets reach respiratory mucosa.

questions.prompt: Which statement about virulence factors is FALSE?

options.text: Siderophores pull iron from host cells.
Fimbriae help E. coli adhere to bladder cells.
IgA protease destroys antibodies in mucus.
Invasins let Salmonella enter host cells.
Kinase helps S. aureus build a clot barricade.

questions.explanation: Coagulase builds the clot (S. aureus); kinase dissolves clots (S. pyogenes).

questions.prompt: Which bacterium and toxin type are correctly paired?

options.text: S. pyogenes — Type III A-B toxin
C. botulinum — Type II hemolysin
S. aureus — Type I superantigen
E. coli — Type I exotoxin as LPS

questions.explanation: S. pyogenes = hemolysin; C. botulinum = A-B; LPS is an endotoxin.

questions.prompt: Explain why healthcare facilities are prone to HAIs and name the two most common HAI types and one major organism.
questions.explanation: They have many reservoirs (sick patients), many invasive procedures (catheters, surgery), and many compromised hosts. The most common HAIs are UTIs (often catheter biofilms) and surgical-site infections; S. aureus/MRSA is a major culprit (also C. diff, Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, Enterococcus).

questions.prompt: Describe Émile Roux's experiment and what it revealed.
questions.explanation: He grew diphtheria in broth, filtered out the cells, and injected the cell-free filtrate into guinea pigs. Young (24–48 h) cultures had no effect, but filtrate from ~2-week cultures killed guinea pigs at tiny doses — revealing a secreted toxin (diphtheria exotoxin) that explained the disease's body-wide effects.

questions.prompt: Why are guinea pigs and filtrates both central to the discovery of diphtheria toxin AND humoral immunity?

options.text: Roux found toxin in a filtrate; von Behring transferred immunity in blood
Both experiments proved Koch's postulates for HIV and AIDS
Both used guinea pigs to grow pure cultures of diphtheria
Both men used filtered viruses to infect their guinea pigs

questions.explanation: Links Module 19 to Module 22.

questions.prompt: Which observation would show that a disease spreads by a biological rather than mechanical vector?

options.text: The pathogen multiplies inside the insect before transmission
The insect lands on food after it has visited garbage
The insect turns out to be non-living, like a fomite
The pathogen is found stuck to the hairs on the insect's legs

questions.explanation: Reproduction inside the vector defines biological transmission.

questions.prompt: Which physical-barrier failure is matched with the right consequence?

options.text: Destroyed ciliary escalator — mucus builds up and is coughed out
Blocked lacrimal duct — stomach acid rises and burns the throat
Loss of sebum — the lacrimal glands stop forming tears
Loss of gastric acid — skin becomes salty and dries out

questions.explanation: Smoking or pertussis toxin can destroy cilia.

questions.prompt: Which list pairs each fluid with its protective chemical correctly?

options.text: Saliva — HCl; tears — sebum; gastric juice — lysozyme
Tears — lysozyme; gastric juice — HCl; vaginal secretions — lactic acid
Sweat — HCl; earwax — lysozyme only; sebum — IgA
Tears — HCl; saliva — sebum; urine — lactic acid

questions.explanation: Saliva adds IgA; earwax and skin rely on sebum.

questions.prompt: Which statement about inflammation is FALSE?

options.text: Histamine constricts vessels, which raises blood pressure.
Redness and heat come from increased blood flow.
Leaky vessels let fluid and WBCs into tissue.
Mast cells release histamine when damaged.
Clotting helps wall in the infection.

questions.explanation: Histamine is a vasodilator that lowers blood pressure.

questions.prompt: Which order shows phagocytosis by a macrophage?

options.text: Pseudopods → exocytosis → phagosome → binding → phagolysosome
Bind via Toll-like receptor → pseudopods → phagosome → phagolysosome → exocytosis
Phagolysosome → binding → pseudopods → phagosome → exocytosis
Exocytosis → binding → phagosome → pseudopods → phagolysosome

questions.explanation: Digest inside the phagolysosome, then expel waste.

questions.prompt: Explain why intact skin is called the body's best defense and describe two features that make it inhospitable to microbes.
questions.explanation: Few pathogens can penetrate it, and it covers nearly every surface. It is dry (little moisture), salty (sweat residue), acidic (sebum fatty acids, pH ~3–5), constantly shedding, and colonized by S. epidermidis, which outcompetes pathogens.

questions.prompt: Compare neutrophils and macrophages at an infection site.
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are first responders that phagocytize immediately but die from overeating (becoming pus). Monocytes arrive and become macrophages, which eat more bacteria without dying because they digest them and exocytose the waste; they also clean up pus and debris.

questions.prompt: Metchnikoff's two major contributions were:

options.text: Discovering antibodies and clonal selection
Discovering penicillin and lysozyme
Inventing pasteurization and the Gram stain
Discovering phagocytes/phagocytosis and promoting probiotics

questions.explanation: Nobel 1908; buttermilk and Lactobacillus.

questions.prompt: Which is a first-line defense rather than a second-line defense?

options.text: Complement activation
Fever
Lysozyme in tears
Phagocytosis

questions.explanation: Antimicrobial chemicals are first line.

questions.prompt: Which complement outcome directly increases the efficiency of phagocytosis?

options.text: Histamine release from mast cells
Opsonization by C3b
Fever from interleukins
MAC formation by C9

questions.explanation: Macrophages have C3b receptors.

questions.prompt: Which statement about complement is FALSE?

options.text: Mannose and LPS can trigger complement.
Complement can trigger inflammation.
Complement proteins circulate inactive in serum.
Complement proteins are made by plasma cells.
Antibodies can trigger complement.

questions.explanation: Complement proteins are serum proteins, not antibodies from plasma cells.

questions.prompt: Pyrogenic interleukins raise body temperature by acting on the:

options.text: Bone marrow
Thymus
Hypothalamus
Lacrimal glands

questions.explanation: They reset the thermostat.

questions.prompt: Which observation best fits interferon's mechanism?

options.text: Cells near an infected cell resist a virus because they've made AVPs
Bacteria near the infected cell burst
Mast cells release histamine near the virus
The infected cell recovers after making interferon

questions.explanation: Interferon protects neighbors, not the producer.

questions.prompt: Describe the membrane attack complex and its outcome.
questions.explanation: Activated C5b recruits C6, C7, C8, and C9; they insert into the bacterial membrane and C9 forms a ring-shaped pore. Several pores cause the cell to lyse (cytolysis).

questions.prompt: Why might a doctor let a low-grade fever run its course, but act quickly on a very high one?
questions.explanation: A low-grade fever impairs bacterial enzymes (which fall off more steeply above 37 °C) while human enzymes still work. Around 44–46 °C, human enzymes denature too, which can be fatal.

questions.prompt: Which second-line defense targets viruses inside cells rather than bacteria?

options.text: Lysozyme
The membrane attack complex
Interferon
Opsonization

questions.explanation: AVPs destroy viral RNA.

questions.prompt: Which complement fragment pairs are matched to the right job?

options.text: C5a — MAC; C3b — mast cells; C9 — opsonin
C3b — pyrogen; C5a — interferon; C9 — AVP
C3a — opsonin; C3b — MAC; C9 — mast cells
C3b — opsonin; C3a/C5a — mast cell triggers; C5b–C9 — MAC

questions.explanation: The three outcomes in fragment form.

questions.prompt: Which antibody structure feature allows agglutination?

options.text: A single heavy chain
Disulfide bonds in the stem
Two antigen-binding sites on each antibody
A constant region that binds mast cells

questions.explanation: Each antibody can bridge two pathogens.

questions.prompt: Which statement about antibody classes is FALSE?

options.text: IgG makes up about 80% of serum antibody.
IgD's function is still unclear.
IgA is the most abundant serum antibody.
IgE sits on the surface of mast cells.
IgM is secreted as a pentamer.

questions.explanation: IgE is a monomer on mast cells; IgA is in breast milk.

questions.prompt: A titer graph shows IgM rising at day 7 and IgG later, then both falling. What does it show?

options.text: A secondary response
Passive immunity
A T-independent memory response
A primary response

questions.explanation: IgM comes first after a lag.

questions.prompt: Which immunity type does each give: antivenom, measles infection, breast milk, flu shot?

options.text: Natural active; artificial passive; artificial active; natural passive
Artificial active; natural passive; natural active; artificial passive
Natural passive; artificial active; natural active; artificial passive
Artificial passive; natural active; natural passive; artificial active

questions.explanation: Who makes the antibodies, and how was the antigen/antibody delivered?

questions.prompt: Describe clonal selection, including what makes the response faster the second time.
questions.explanation: Billions of B cells each have a unique receptor; an antigen binds and selects the matching B cell, which clones into plasma cells (secrete antibodies) and memory cells. On re-exposure, the many memory cells respond immediately, producing more IgG faster.

questions.prompt: Explain how antibodies can trigger inflammation and why IgG can't.
questions.explanation: Antigen binding to IgE anchored on mast cells (via their constant-region receptors) triggers histamine release → inflammation. Mast cell receptors fit only IgE's constant region, so IgG can't.

questions.prompt: Von Behring's transferred immunity lasted about three weeks. Which modern treatment works the same way?

options.text: Receiving an attenuated MMR vaccine
Recovering from chickenpox
Receiving a toxoid vaccine
Injecting monoclonal antibodies

questions.explanation: Both are passive — preformed antibodies.

questions.prompt: Which pair of scientists and contributions is correct?

options.text: Burnet — clonal selection; von Behring — humoral immunity
Koch — antibodies; Roux — clonal selection
Metchnikoff — clonal selection; Burnet — phagocytes
Burnet — humoral immunity; von Behring — clonal selection

questions.explanation: Nobel Prizes 1960 and 1901.

questions.prompt: Which list includes only antigen-presenting cells that use MHC-2?

options.text: Skin cells, liver cells, B cells
Neutrophils, red blood cells, mast cells
Cytotoxic T cells, NK cells, eosinophils
Macrophages, dendritic cells, B cells

questions.explanation: Regular body cells use MHC-1.

questions.prompt: Which statement is FALSE?

options.text: CD8 on helper T cells binds MHC-2.
T cells mature in the thymus.
CD4 on helper T cells binds MHC-2.
CD8 on cytotoxic T cells binds MHC-1.
T cell receptors are never secreted.

questions.explanation: Helper T cells carry CD4, not CD8.

questions.prompt: A cytotoxic T cell kills a virus-infected cell. Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Viral antigen on MHC-2 → TCR + CD4 bind → interleukin → plasma cells
C3b on cell → macrophage → phagolysosome → exocytosis
Antibody on cell → Fc receptor → histamine → inflammation
Viral antigen on MHC-1 → TCR + CD8 bind → perforin and granzyme → apoptosis

questions.explanation: The killer T cell pathway.

questions.prompt: Why does HIV cause a low WBC count and widespread immune failure?

options.text: It blocks interferon in every cell
It destroys red blood cells, lowering all counts
It destroys MHC-1, so NK cells attack all cells
It destroys helper T cells, which coordinate B cell activation

questions.explanation: Helper T cells are central to adaptive immunity.

questions.prompt: Explain how NK cells use two different receptors to choose targets.
questions.explanation: Fc receptors bind antibody constant regions on coated targets (parasites) → antibody-dependent cytotoxicity. MHC-1 receptors detect self; binding MHC-1 inhibits the NK cell, so cells lacking MHC-1 (e.g., some cancer cells) are killed with perforin and granzymes.

questions.prompt: Explain how monoclonal antibodies are made and give one diagnostic and one therapeutic use.
questions.explanation: Inject an antigen into a mouse → isolate the B cell making the desired antibody → fuse it with an immortal cancer cell (ethylene glycol) → hybridoma secretes identical antibodies indefinitely. Diagnostic: rapid COVID/pregnancy/strep tests. Therapeutic: cancer 'magic bullets' or COVID monoclonals that neutralize the spike protein.

questions.prompt: Which difference between apoptosis and necrosis matters most for inflammation?

options.text: Apoptosis is caused by bacteria; necrosis is caused by cytotoxic T cells
Apoptotic cells call macrophages to clean up; necrosis spills and inflames
Necrosis is programmed cell death; apoptosis is an accidental death
Apoptosis only happens in cancer cells; necrosis happens in all others

questions.explanation: Tidy vs messy cell death.

questions.prompt: On a rapid antigen test, no line appears at C or T. What is the result?

options.text: Negative
Invalid
Positive
Positive for a different virus

questions.explanation: A control line is always required.

questions.prompt: Which list puts smallpox prevention in historical order?

options.text: Jenner's cowpox → Chinese scab inhalation → European variolation → Pasteur
Pasteur → Jenner → variolation → Chinese inhalation
Chinese scab inhalation → European variolation → Jenner's cowpox → Pasteur coins 'vaccine'
European variolation → Pasteur → Chinese inhalation → Jenner

questions.explanation: 1400s → 1700s → Jenner → Pasteur.

questions.prompt: Which vaccine pairing is FALSE?

options.text: Tetanus — toxoid
HPV — attenuated whole agent
Rabies — inactivated whole agent
MMR — attenuated whole agent
COVID — nucleic acid

questions.explanation: HPV is a subunit vaccine.

questions.prompt: Which drug pairing of target and mechanism is correct?

options.text: Erythromycin — protein synthesis; vancomycin — cell wall
Sulfanilamide — protein synthesis; tetracycline — folic acid
Cipro — cell wall; penicillin — DNA gyrase
Cephalosporin — nucleic acid; streptomycin — enzyme function

questions.explanation: The four lecture targets.

questions.prompt: Why are DNA COVID vaccines better for remote parts of the world?

options.text: They stay stable at room temperature and need only one dose
They use lipid nanoparticles that never break down
They contain live coronavirus that spreads protection
They don't require any injection

questions.explanation: mRNA needs ultra-cold storage and two doses.

questions.prompt: Compare Ehrlich's and Fleming's contributions to antimicrobial therapy.
questions.explanation: Ehrlich pioneered synthetic antimicrobials with 'magic bullets' — Preparation 606 (Salvarsan, arsenic + dye) treated trypanosomes and syphilis. Fleming discovered penicillin from Penicillium mold's zone of inhibition; Chain and Florey later mass-produced it during WWII.

questions.prompt: Explain when to use broad- versus narrow-spectrum antibiotics and why.
questions.explanation: Broad-spectrum when the pathogen is unknown (they hit many bacteria but also kill normal flora, risking superinfections and resistance). Narrow-spectrum when the pathogen is known, to target it while sparing normal flora.

questions.prompt: Which new approach to resistant infections is self-amplifying and self-eliminating?

options.text: Phage therapy
Broad-spectrum antibiotics
Quorum-sensing inhibitors
Variolation

questions.explanation: Phages multiply only while their target bacteria remain.

questions.prompt: A quorum-sensing inhibitor would most likely stop which outcome?

options.text: Bacteria forming endospores in dry soil
Bacteria taking up plasmids by conjugation
A large bacterial population releasing toxins all at once
A single bacterium dividing by binary fission

questions.explanation: It blocks the signal that coordinates toxin release.
